q7.answer: Shared presence state lives in the Redis primary, not in any gateway's memory. Membership is one sorted-set member per connection (presence:doc:{docId}, member connId, score = lease deadline in ms). Identity is one hash per connection (presence:conn:{connId}, TTL 30 s). Caret is one hash per user (presence:caret:{docId}:{userId}, TTL 30 s). Each node's 10 s heartbeat refreshes only its own connections: it sets the lease score to now plus 30 s, resets the conn and caret TTLs, and extends the sorted-set key to 60 s.

q8.answer: A crashed node runs no cleanup. Its leases stop being extended, so its conn and caret hashes expire by TTL about 30 s after the last heartbeat. Any surviving node with a local socket on the document sweeps the sorted set every 10 s, reading expired members with ZRANGEBYSCORE and removing each with ZREM. Only the node whose ZREM returns 1 publishes the presence leave hint, so exactly one announcement goes out. Other clients then re-read the snapshot and drop the user, with worst case about 40 s.

q9.answer: The accepting node writes the caret to Redis (HINCRBY seq, HSET pos and rev, PEXPIRE 30 s) and PUBLISHes {userId, seq, pos, rev} on cursor:doc:{docId}. Every node subscribed to that channel, which is any node with a local socket on the document, forwards it to its local clients, so a viewer on another node gets it through pub/sub. A viewer on the sender's own node gets it the same way, through its own subscription to the channel. The diagram shows only the cross-node path, so the same-node path is implied by the subscription rule rather than drawn.

q10.answer: The joiner's node subscribes to the presence and cursor channels before it reads state, and the snapshot is read from the Redis primary rather than from pub/sub history. Any join or leave that happens during loading therefore either shows up in the snapshot or arrives as a hint after subscription, and every hint triggers a fresh re-read. A missed cursor message is harmless because the next move corrects it.

q11.answer: The joining client sends an initial cursor right after open, which writes the user's caret hash even if they never move. The snapshot includes each listed user's last caret from the caret hash, so the joiner draws idle users at once. The heartbeat refreshes the caret TTL for every local user, so an idle user's caret stays alive.

q12.answer: Each cursor carries a per-user seq that HINCRBY increments, and the receiver keeps the last shown seq per userId and drops any caret whose seq is not higher, so out-of-order messages cannot move a caret back. Carets with rev above appliedRev are held, keeping only the highest-seq one per user, and drawn when appliedRev reaches that rev. Carets at or below appliedRev are transformed forward with transformPosition, and the stored position is updated to the new rev. The open gap is that seq resets if the caret hash is lost while the user is still listed, which this answer does not fix.
